# Brief Statement of the Relevant Facts of the Project

## The Intervention Recommender Tool for Heijmans Vastgoed

Heijmans Vastgoed, a Dutch property developer, uses well-being impact scans to identify opportunities in neighborhoods. The scans show where opportunities lie but does not recommend which interventions fit. Our team developed an Intervention Recommender Tool to close this gap: a decision-support application that for a given neighborhood ranks well-being interventions using a weighted scoring model. The model is transparent to its users: they see each intervention's scores and can adjust the weights of the criteria.[^1]

[^1]: [@Heijmans2026, sections 1-3]

The tool runs on a structured database of interventions. It combines interventions collected by the team together with the high priority interventions from a list that Heijmans supplied as an Excel file. Each intervention is classified by theme and scored on criteria such as impact, cost, effort, risk and feasibility. The initial scores were generated with generative AI and then reviewed and adjusted manually by the team.[^2] Users see the outcome, not the source code. The tool is intended to support consultants, not replace them, and to be scalable across projects.[^3]

[^2]: [@Heijmans2026, sections 3.2-3.4, 4].

[^3]: [@Heijmans2026, sections 2, 7].

This report assesses the project in an operational scenario. The following assumptions scope the assignment, not all of them were part of the original project:

1.  The team acts as a Dutch data consultancy hired by Heijmans. The proposal covers scope and fees for all project work and contains a mutual confidentiality clause: each party keeps the others information confidential and uses it only for the project. It says nothing about who owns, or may license, the database or the tool.
2.  Heijmans collected the interventions on its list over several years from its past projects and partners, and structured them by theme and priority. Its employees wrote the impact scans. Neither is public, and both were shared with the consultancy under the confidentiality clause only.
3.  To fill gaps, the consultancy plans to add most of the interventions from a third-party online library, collected by a scraper. The library is run by a Dutch organisation whose editorial team collects, checks and updates the interventions. It is free to use, but only after registering an account and accepting terms of use, which prohibit automated access and extraction. The site's robots.txt reserves the same rights.
4.  Heijmans wants to reuse the tool and the combined database across its own projects and to offer them commercially to third parties, such as housing corporations and municipalities. The consultancy wants to reuse the generic parts of the tool, its code and scoring model, for other clients.

# Analysis of IP Rights Protection

Based on the case description above, this section tests five assets against each right:

| Asset | Protected by | Rightholder |
|:------------------------|:----------------------|:------------------------|
| \(A\) Heijmans' intervention list | Sui generis right; trade secret | Heijmans |
| \(B\) Impact scans | Copyright; trade secret | Heijmans |
| \(C\) Third-party library | Sui generis right | Library maker |
| \(D\) Combined database | Sui generis right (collection layer only); Scores unprotected | Heijmans (likely) |
| \(E\) Source code & model | Copyright and trade secret (source code only); scoring model unprotected | Consultancy |

: Overview of IP protection per asset {#tbl-ip-overview}

## Database rights

A database is a collection of independent materials, arranged systematically and individually accessible.[^4] The intervention list (A), the library (C) and the combined database (D) fit this definition: each consists of separate interventions that can be retrieved one by one. The impact scans (B) do not. Each scan is one integrated analysis of a neighborhood whose parts have no autonomous informative value, so they are assessed under copyright and trade secrets only.

[^4]: Art. 1(2) [@DatabaseDirective1996]; Art. 1(1)(a) Dbw; [@FixturesOPAP2004].

Database copyright requires the selection or arrangement of the contents to be the author's own intellectual creation. Labour and skill spent on the data itself are irrelevant.[^5] Grouping interventions by theme, category or priority and scoring them on standard criteria is functional and leaves little room for creative choices, so none of the three databases qualifies.

[^5]: Art. 3(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996]; Art. 10(3) Aw; [@FootballDatacoYahoo2012].

The sui generis right instead rewards a substantial investment in obtaining, verifying or presenting the contents rather than in creating them.[^6] Heijmans, the consultancy and the library's maker are all Dutch, so the condition in Art.11 is met.[^7] Heijmans collected its list (A) over several years from past projects and partners and structured it by theme and priority (investment in obtaining and presenting existing material), so the list is protected with Heijmans as the maker. The library (C) is protected as well: its editorial team collects, checks and updates the interventions. For the combined database (D), the consultancy's work in collecting and presenting interventions from several sources counts, but the scores do not: generating and then reviewing them is the creation of new data.[^8] A sui generis right therefore exists in the collection layer only. Its maker is whoever took the initiative and bore the risk of the investment. [^9] Although Heijmans commissioned the tool rather than the database, it pays the fees for all project work, so it bears the investment risk and is likely the maker.

[^6]: Art. 7(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996]; Art. 2 Dbw; [@BHB2004].

[^7]: Art. 11 [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^8]: [@BHB2004].

[^9]: Recital 41 [@DatabaseDirective1996]; Art. 1(1)(b) Dbw.

## Copyright

A work is protected if it is the author's own intellectual creation, reflecting free and creative choices.[^10] Ideas, methods of operation and the principles underlying a computer program are not. [^11]

[^10]: [@Infopaq2009]; CJEU 12 September 2019, C-683/17 (*Cofemel*).

[^11]: Art. 9(2) TRIPS; Art. 1(2) Directive 2009/24/EC; [@SAS2012].

The impact scans (B) meet this test: their authors chose how to combine text, analysis, maps and recommendations. Protection covers that expression, not the facts and findings. Because Heijmans' employees wrote the scans as part of their work, Heijmans is treated as the author and holds the copyright.[^12]

[^12]: Art. 7 Aw.

The source code (E) is protected as a computer program. It was written by the consultancy's employees, so the consultancy holds the copyright; commissioning and paying for the tool does not transfer it to Heijmans.[^13] The scoring model (E) is not protected: its criteria, weights and ranking logic are ideas and methods of operation. The scores (D) are not protected either, the AI-generated baseline has no human author, and adjusting a numeric score is not a creative choice.

[^13]: Art. 2(3) Directive 2009/24/EC; Arts. 2(2), 7 and 10(1)(12) Aw.

## Trade Secrets

Information is a trade secret if it is secret, has commercial value because it is secret, and is subject to reasonable steps to keep it secret.[^14] Heijmans' list (A) and scans (B) meet all three conditions: they are not public, they reveal where Heijmans sees development opportunities, and the consultancy received them under a confidentiality clause. This covers their content, including the findings that copyright leaves free, which makes it Heijmans' strongest right. The source code (E) meets the same conditions: it is not public, users see only its outcome, and its value lies in a working tool that competitors cannot simply copy, and the mutal confidentiality clause binds Heijmans. The scoring model and the scores do not: users see them and adjust weights, so they are not secret. Because the proposal is silent on ownership, the consultancy remains the holder, as it developed the code and controls it.[^15]

[^14]: Art. 2(1) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016]; Art. 1 Wbb.

[^15]: Art. 2(2) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

# Assessment of Barriers and Infringement

## Using Heijmans’ list and scans

Within the Heijmans project, using the intervention list (A) and the impact scans (B) carries no real risk. The consultancy performs two acts: it copies the priority interventions from the list into the combined database, and it derives interventions from the findings of the scans.

Taking the high priority interventions is an extraction of a substantial part, at least qualitatively, as these are the entries Heijmans itself rated most important. This normally requires the maker's authorisation.[^16] Heijmans supplied the list precisely so that it could be built into the tool, so that authorisation is given, at least for the purpose of the project.

[^16]: Art. 7(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

The same reasoning applies to Heijmans' trade secret in A and B. The consultancy acquired the information with the consent of Heijmans, this means that the acquisition is lawful.[^17] Using a lawfully acquired trade secret only becomes unlawful when it breaches a contractual or other duty to limit that use.[^18] The confidentiality clause limits use to the project, and the consultancy stays within that limit.

[^17]: Art. 3(1)(d) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

[^18]: Art. 4(3)(c) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

Copyright in the scans is not engaged. The tool takes over what the scans found, not how their authors expressed it, and copyright protects only the expression of a work, not facts or data as such.[^19]

[^19]: Recital 45 [@DatabaseDirective1996]; [@Infopaq2009].

The real limit lies at the edge of the project. Any use of the list or scans for other clients or products falls outside the confidentiality clause and is assessed in depth in @sec-reuse.

## Scraping the third-party library

As planned, scraping the library infringes its maker's sui generis right and breaches the terms of use.

This is mainly because the scraper copies interventions in bulk into the consultancy's dataset. This is an extraction: a transfer of the contents of a database to another medium,[^20] for which physical copying is not even required.[^21] Because the scraper copies most of the library, the extraction is substantial in quantity. Furthermore the extraction is also substantial in quality, because it takes the contents in which the editorial team invested by collecting, checking and updating them.[^22] Another possible option which is spreading the scraping over many small runs does not suffice to mitigate the infringement: as repeated and systematic extraction of insubstantial parts that conflicts with normal exploitation of the database is prohibited as well.[^23]

[^20]: Art. 7(2)(a) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^21]: [@Directmedia2008].

[^22]: Art. 7(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996]; [@BHB2004].

[^23]: Art. 7(5) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

The exceptions in the Database Directive do not help. As a registered user, the consultancy is a lawful user and is allowed to extract insubstantial parts, a right the maker cannot override by contract,[^24] but this does not cover bulk extraction. The exception for teaching and scientific research is limited to non-commercial purposes, which the consultancy does not pursue.[^25] In addition, the other data mining exception for scientific research is reserved for research organisations and cultural heritage institutions, not a commercial consultancy.[^26]

[^24]: Arts. 8(1) and 15 [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^25]: Art. 9(b) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^26]: Arts. 2(1) and 3 [@DSMDirective2019].

That leaves the general data mining exception, which allows anyone with lawful access to reproduce and extract contents for data mining, for any purpose, as long as the copies are kept only as long as necessary.[^27] The consultancy has lawful access through its account. However, the maker can opt out by expressly reserving its rights. For content made publicly available online, the reservation must be machine-readable; in other cases, a reservation in a contract or unilateral declaration is deemed good enough.[^28] The maker reserves its rights both in its terms of use and in machine-readable form in its robots.txt, so the opt-out is valid whether or not the library counts as publicly available online, and the exception is unavailable. Unlike the research exception, the general exception can be overridden by contract.[^29]

[^27]: Art. 4(1)–(2) [@DSMDirective2019].

[^28]: Art. 4(3) and Recital 18 [@DSMDirective2019].

[^29]: Art. 7(1) [@DSMDirective2019].

Even without the opt-out, Art. 4 would not cover the plan: it permits copies for automated analysis, kept only as long as necessary, whereas the consultancy wants to store the interventions permanently in its database.[^30]

[^30]: Arts. 2(2) and 4(2) [@DSMDirective2019].

The terms of use also create a separate contractual risk. By accepting them, the consultancy agreed not to scrape, and this commitment holds regardless of the outcome under database law. If the library were not protected under the Database Directive, neither its exceptions nor the data mining exceptions would apply, and the maker would be free to restrict use by contract.[^31] Because the library is protected (Section 2.1), the sui generis claim comes on top of the contract claim. The residual risk is therefore a sui generis infringement claim and a breach-of-contract claim, both against the consultancy.

[^31]: [@Ryanair2015].

## Commercial reuse {#sec-reuse}

Commercial reuse is the main barrier, because each party needs rights that the other holds and the proposal does not regulate them. This section builds on the ownership found in Section 2.

Heijmans wants to offer the tool to housing corporations and municipalities. Doing so requires reproducing and distributing the program, which are exclusive acts of the copyright holder, which in this case is the consultancy.[^32] Without a licence, Heijmans cannot do this. If the tool is distributed with its source code, that would also disclose the consultancy's trade secret, which the mutual confidentiality clause prohibits Heijmans from disclosing.[^33] The scoring model is visible to every user and is not protected.

[^32]: Art. 4(1)(a) and (c) Directive 2009/24/EC.

[^33]: Art. 4(3)(b) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

On the other side the consultancy wants to reuse the generic parts of the tool for other clients. It may reuse its own code, and the scoring model, which nobody owns. It may not reuse the combined database (D), because Heijmans is likely its maker and extracting a substantial part requires Heijmans' consent.[^34] Using Heijmans' list (A) or insights from the scans (B) for other clients would breach the duty to limit use to the project, making it an unlawful use of Heijmans' trade secret.[^35]

[^34]: Art. 7(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^35]: Art. 4(3)(c) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

The scraped library content creates a further risk. If scraped interventions end up in D and Heijmans offers D to third parties, that is a re-utilisation of the library's contents.[^36] Heijmans' own sui generis right in D does not help to mitigate this, because protection of a database is without prejudice to rights in its contents.[^37] The library's maker can therefore bring a sui generis claim against both the consultancy and Heijmans. It has a contract claim only against the consultancy, because Heijmans never accepted the terms of use. Heijmans would carry this exposure without knowing it, unless the consultancy discloses where the data came from.

[^36]: Art. 7(2)(b) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^37]: Art. 7(4) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

The residual risk lies in the ownership of D. Section 2.1 concluded that Heijmans is likely the maker, because it funds the work and bears the investment risk. The Database Directive supports this by excluding subcontractors from the definition of maker.[^38] The consultancy could still argue that it took the initiative to build the database, since Heijmans commissioned a tool rather than a database. Until a contract settles this, both parties' reuse plans rest on uncertain ground.

[^38]: Recital 41 [@DatabaseDirective1996].

## Overall assessment

The project can be completed for Heijmans, but not scaled or sold as planned. Two issues block this: scraping the library, which needs its maker's permission or other sources, and commercial reuse, which needs a contract settling ownership and mutual licences. Both cost time, but neither stops the project. Using Heijmans' list and scans within the project, and the team's own scores, are lawful as they stand. The scores and the scoring model are not protected (Sections 2.2 and 2.3), so neither party can stop others from reusing them.

# Advice

This section advises the consultancy, including what it should agree with Heijmans. It follows the two blocking issues from Section 3.4.

## Obtaining data lawfully

The consultancy should not run the scraper as planned. The safest route is a license from the library's maker.[^39] It should cover extraction and storage by the consultancy and re-utilisation by Heijmans towards third parties, as Section 3.3 showed that Heijmans would otherwise be exposed. The trade-offs are a fee, a delay for negotiation, and the risk that the maker refuses or only allows internal use.

[^39]: Art. 7(3) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

If the maker refuses, three lawful alternatives remain. First, public sector information under the Open Data Directive: public bodies must allow re-use, in principle free of charge and under standard licences, and may not use their sui generis right to block it. Documents in which third parties hold IP rights are excluded however, and public data is mostly statistics rather than ready-made interventions.[^40] Protected public data can be requested under the Data Governance Act, but only with a decision period of up to two months.[^41] Second, openly licensed datasets. The consultancy should check what the licence covers and avoid non-commercial and share-alike terms. Third, interventions the team writes itself. Ideas and facts are free, and as lawful user the consultancy may consult the library and take insubstantial parts,[^42] but systematically retyping is still extraction.[^43] This takes the most time, but the result is fully owned.

[^40]: Arts. 1(2)(c), 1(6), 3, 6(1) and 8 [@OpenDataDirective2019].

[^41]: Arts. 3, 5 and 9 [@DataGovernanceAct2022].

[^42]: Recital 45 and Art. 8(1) [@DatabaseDirective1996].

[^43]: Art. 7(5) [@DatabaseDirective1996]; [@Directmedia2008].

Whatever the source, the consultancy should record where each intervention came from and under which terms. That record allows it to give Heijmans a warranty on the data it hands over, which removes the hidden exposure identified in Section 3.3.

## Settling the rights with Heijmans

The entanglement of rights is best resolved in a written agreement before the tool is reused or sold, as copyright can only be transferred by deed.[^44] The agreement should cover three points: 1. The consultancy keeps the copyright in the source code and licenses Heijmans to use the tool and offer it to third parties, preferably as an online service or in object code, so that the source code is not handed over. A licence fee or royalty can reflect its commercial value. 2. Heijmans is confirmed as maker of the database (D), in return for a licence-back allowing the consultancy to extract the interventions it contributed and reuse them for other clients. 3. The confidentiality clause continues to limit use of Heijmans' list and scans to Heijmans' projects. For other clients, the consultancy builds a separate version without that data.

[^44]: Art. 2(2) Aw.

The scores and the scoring model remain unprotected: the contract binds only the two parties, so neither can use them as an exclusive asset against competitors.

## Protecting the source code

Because copyright protects the expression of the code and not its functionality[^45] competitors may build a similar tool. The consultancy's advantage therefore lies in keeping the code secret: keeping it out of client deliveries, binding employees and contractors with access through non-disclosure agreements, and restricting access on a need-to-know basis. Licence terms can prohibit copying, but not observing and testing the program or decompiling it for interoperability.[^46] These measures also count as the reasonable steps trade secret protection requires.[^47]

[^45]: [@SAS2012].

[^46]: Arts. 5(3), 6 and 8 Directive 2009/24/EC.

[^47]: Art. 2(1)(c) [@TradeSecretsDirective2016].

## Conclusion

The tool can be completed and used for Heijmans as planned. To scale and sell it, the consultancy should first drop the scraping plan and agree the rigths with Heijmans, and then license the library or replace its data with open or self-written sources. If no agreement with Heijmans is reached, the fallback is to retrict the tool to Heijmans and rebuild the generic core for other clients form independent sources.
